newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: FORECAST - Irish exchequer seen moving into black.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Irish exchequer seen moving into black.

text.p: For the first time in decades, the Irish government is expected to be in the black, showing a cumulative running surplus, when end-September Exchequer Returns data is published on Wednesday.
Economists are forecasting anything from zero to a 175 million punt surplus as timing factors and a robust economy kick in to boost the Exchequer's coffers.
"I am expecting an Exchequer surplus of 175 million punts. On a rational basis I see it around this level or higher," Goodbody stockbrokers economist Han de Jong told Reuters.

Bloxham stockbrokers' Alan McQuaid expects a cumulative running Exchequer surplus of 75 million punts while Dan McLaughlin, economist with Riada stockbrokers, is going for a cautious zero borrowing requirement.
The Exchequer Borrowing Requirement (EBR) in the first half of 1996 was 455 million compared with 561 million at the end of the first quarter to March.

The Government target borrowing requirement, set in its February annual budget, was 729 million punts but the Department of Finance indicated at the half-year stage that it was likely to undershoot that target and some economists believe the full-year borrowing requirement may be below 500 million punts.

While such a benign borrowing position allows the authorities scope to stimulate economic growth through tax cuts in what will be an election budget in early 1997, such a move may lead to unwanted inflationary pressures, economists say.
On Thursday, Central Bank monthly statistics are expected to confirm a worryingly strong credit growth position.
Riada's McLaughlin expects credit growth at 14.1 percent while Goodbodys' de Jong is going for underlying credit growth of 13.8 percent for August against 13.7 percent in July.
De Jong expects mortgage lending to accelerate to 16.4 percent from 16.1 percent in July and McLaughlin is going for a more moderate 16.2 percent.

Both economists believe the central bank will be far from happy with such strong growth levels but its hands are tied as it tries to balance the Irish currency against its European counterparts while containing interest rates and inflationary pressures.

"I don't think the central bank will be comfortable with that growth rate," McLaughlin said. "They indicated at the start of the year they wanted credit growth in single digits, instead it has been accelerating, especially on the mortgage side."
Further stimuli to growth could push Ireland's inflation level to the outer edge of Maastricht requirements in a year when the EU takes stock of who qualifies.
"It would be ironic if Ireland failed to qualify for EMU after years of being comfortably within the Maastricht criteria," Riada's McLaughlin said.
Ireland's inflation level in the first half of 1996 was a comfortable 1.5 percent. Bloxham's McQuaid expects this to move up to 2.5 percent in 1997 which may trigger warning bells.

Maastricht criteria requires qualifying countries to have inflation rates of not more than 1.5 percentage points above the average of the three best performing countries. McQuaid estimates the current EU inflation average at 1.1 to 1.3 pct.
